t: The rebellious one or the rebellious house?
p: The Hebrew has 'the rebellious one'; Swete's Greek has the usual 'rebellious house'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: to the rebellious one
readings.plain: the rebellious one

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: to the rebellious house
readings.plain: the rebellious house

why: The Hebrew, read without change, is 'to the rebellious one, to the house of Israel'. The Plain English Translation follows it. The Greek has the phrase Ezekiel uses elsewhere (2:5-8; 3:9, 26-27), which may reflect a Hebrew text with beit meri, or a translator smoothing the phrase. The Plain English Translation's wording elsewhere is 'rebellious house'; see the note.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse. The Plain English Translation's usual wording for the phrase elsewhere in Ezekiel is 'rebellious house'.

p: The Hebrew says 'fat and blood'; Swete's Greek says 'loaves, flesh and blood'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: fat and blood
readings.plain: the fat

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: loaves, flesh and blood
readings.plain: the flesh

why: 'Fat and blood' is the usual priestly pair of the parts of a sacrifice that belong to the LORD (Leviticus 3:16-17), and 44:15 has the same pair. The Greek reads 'flesh' here, but 'fat and blood' in 44:15, so the Greek translator is not simply following a different Hebrew word throughout.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

t: A dispute or a case of blood?
p: Swete's Greek has 'a judgment of blood'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a dispute
readings.plain: a dispute

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: a judgment of blood
readings.plain: a case of bloodshed

why: The Hebrew word riv, 'dispute', is the usual word for a legal quarrel (Deuteronomy 17:8; 19:17). The Greek's 'blood' may come from a different Hebrew word or may be a free reading. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: It will be 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 wide.
p: The Hebrew gives 10,000 for the width; Swete's Greek gives 20,000 in 45:1, 3 and 5.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: ten thousand
readings.plain: It will be 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 wide.

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: a breadth of twenty thousand
readings.plain: It will be 25,000 cubits long and 20,000 wide.

why: The Hebrew follows the text as it stands, and the Plain English Translation keeps it. But the Hebrew does not add up: in 45:1 the whole district is said to be 25,000 by 10,000, and in 45:3 and 45:5 the priests' strip and the Levites' strip are each 25,000 by 10,000, so two strips of 10,000 cannot fit into one strip of 10,000. The Greek reads 20,000 in 45:1, which makes the total work (10,000 for the priests plus 10,000 for the Levites), and so does its 20,000 in 48:13. But the same Greek also reads 20,000 for each strip in 45:3 and 45:5, which does not fit its own 45:1, and 48:10 and 48:13 give each strip as 10,000 in Hebrew and Greek alike. The totals therefore work only on the Greek, and the strips only on the Hebrew. A single Greek witness that smooths a difficulty is weaker evidence than it looks, and no scroll preserves the verse, so the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and the note says why.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse. See also 45:3, 45:5 and 48:9.

p: Swete's Greek has 20,000 here too; goes with 45:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a width of ten thousand
readings.plain: 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 wide

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: and a width of twenty thousand
readings.plain: 25,000 cubits long and 20,000 wide

why: Same reasoning as 45:1; the two verses go together. The Greek's 20,000 here conflicts with 48:10 and 48:13, where the strip is 10,000 in both Hebrew and Greek. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

t: Twenty rooms or cities to live in?
p: Swete's Greek has 'cities to live in'; its width is 20,000.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: twenty rooms
readings.plain: with twenty rooms

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: cities to live in
readings.plain: with cities to live in

why: 'Twenty rooms' is the Hebrew as it stands, and it is odd for a district of land. The Greek's 'cities to live in' may reflect a Hebrew 'arim lashevet, which some commentators prefer because it matches the Levites' cities in Numbers 35:1-8. The Greek also reads 20,000 for the width in this verse (see 45:1). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: Your mina will be made up of twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels and fifteen shekels.
t: Sixty shekels in the mina, or other numbers?
p: Swete's Greek has different numbers for the mina, and its middle phrase is incomplete.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: עֶשְׂרִים שְׁקָלִים חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים שְׁקָלִים עֲשָׂרָה וַחֲמִשָּׁה שֶׁקֶל (esrim shekalim, chamishah ve'esrim shekalim, asarah vachamishah shekel)
readings.en: twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, fifteen shekels: the mina
readings.plain: Your mina will be made up of twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels and fifteen shekels.

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.orig: πέντε σίκλοι, πέντε καὶ σίκλοι, δέκα καὶ πεντήκοντα σίκλοι ἡ μνᾶ
readings.en: five shekels, 'five and' shekels, 'ten and fifty' shekels: the mina
readings.plain: Your mina will be made up of five shekels, 'five and' shekels and 'ten and fifty' shekels.

why: The Hebrew gives 20 + 25 + 15 = 60, the Babylonian mina. The Greek has other numbers, and its second term ('five and ... shekels') reads as if a number has dropped out, so it gives no clear sum. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: From each flock of 200 in the well-watered land of Israel
p: Swete's Greek has 'one sheep out of ten' and 'from all the families of Israel'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: from the two hundred, from the well-watered land of Israel
readings.plain: From each flock of 200 in the well-watered land of Israel

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.orig: ἀπὸ δέκα, ἀφαίρεμα ἐκ πασῶν τῶν πατριῶν τοῦ Ἰσραήλ
readings.en: from ten, a levy from all the families of Israel
readings.plain: From each flock of ten, taken from all the families of Israel

why: One sheep in 200 matches the very low rates of 45:13-14 (one-sixtieth of grain, one-hundredth of oil). One in ten would be a tithe and is out of scale with those. The Greek 'families' (patriai) may stand for mishpachot where the Hebrew has mishqeh, 'well-watered land'. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: on the seventh day of the month
t: The seventh day, or the first of the seventh month?
p: Swete's Greek names the seventh month and its first day.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: on the seventh of the month
readings.plain: on the seventh day of the month

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ἑβδόμῳ μηνὶ μιᾷ τοῦ μηνός
readings.en: in the seventh month, on the first of the month
readings.plain: in the seventh month, on the first day of the month

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, the only Hebrew witness. The Greek reading is clear: a second cleansing six months after the first, in the autumn, which is near the Day of Atonement season. The Talmud knows only the reading 'seventh' and asks what the seventh is for (Menachot 45a).
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

p: Swete's Greek has no word for 'weeks'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a festival, weeks of days
readings.plain: a festival of seven days

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: a festival; seven days
readings.plain: a festival of seven days

why: The Hebrew 'weeks' is hard in this place, where the festival is Unleavened Bread. A common proposal is to read shiv'at, 'seven of', for shevu'ot. The Greek has only 'seven days', which gives the same meaning as the Plain English Translation, and so there is no change of wording. The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew in the sense the Greek confirms.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

p: The Hebrew has the 'eastern district'; Swete's Greek transliterates it as Galilee.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the eastern district
readings.plain: the eastern district

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: Galilee, the one to the east
readings.plain: Galilee, the part to the east

why: The Hebrew word gelilah is a common noun for a district (Joshua 13:2; 22:10-11). The Greek takes it as the proper name Galilee. The river goes down to the Arabah and the Salt Sea, in the south, so a Galilee in the north would not fit. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

p: The Hebrew has a dual 'two rivers'; Swete's Greek has 'the river'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: two rivers
readings.plain: the two rivers

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: the river
readings.plain: the river

why: The dual is unusual in Hebrew and the verse ends with the single 'the river' (hannachal). It may be a scribal slip for the plural or singular, or it may be a real dual for the river's two banks or two branches. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew as the harder reading.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: from the border to the eastern sea you will measure
t: 'You will measure', or 'as far as Tamar'?
p: The Hebrew ends the clause with a verb, tammodu, 'you will measure'; Swete's Greek has a place name.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: you will measure
readings.plain: from the border to the eastern sea you will measure

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: of the palm grove (that is, Tamar)
readings.plain: down to the eastern sea, as far as Tamar

why: The Hebrew word is a verb, tammodu 'you will measure', and the Plain English Translation follows it. The Greek has Phoinikonos, 'of the palm grove', a rendering of Tamar (tamar, 'date palm'), which is the place named in 47:19 and 48:28. Many readers take Tamar here, which would be a change of resh for dalet and of the ending. The Plain English Translation does not make the change: no Hebrew witness read for this part has Tamar, and the Greek may be a translator's way of making sense of a hard verb.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

t: Ten thousand or twenty-five thousand wide?
p: The Hebrew gives 10,000 for the width; Swete's Greek makes the verse the whole square.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the contribution that you set apart for the LORD: length twenty-five thousand, width ten thousand
readings.plain: 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 wide

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: the contribution: length twenty-five thousand, width twenty-five thousand
readings.plain: 25,000 cubits long and 25,000 wide

why: The Hebrew has 10,000, with the same words ('the contribution that you set apart') that 48:8 and 48:20 use for the whole district. Read by itself, 48:9 therefore names the whole district and gives it a width that fits only the priests' strip (48:10). To say that 48:9 'describes the priests' strip' is to harmonize it, which the Hebrew does not say. The Greek has 25,000, which makes 48:9 the whole square, as 48:20 has it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew; see the note at 48:9 and the sums in the note at 48:8.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: It will measure 25,000 cubits along the north, 10,000 along the west, 10,000 along the east, and 25,000 along the south.
p: Swete's Greek lists three sides, not four.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: northward 25,000; westward breadth 10,000; eastward breadth 10,000; southward length 25,000
readings.plain: It will measure 25,000 cubits along the north, 10,000 along the west, 10,000 along the east, and 25,000 along the south.

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.orig: πρὸς βορρᾶν... πρὸς θάλασσαν... πρὸς νότον
readings.en: toward the north 25,000; toward the sea 10,000; toward the south 25,000
readings.plain: It will measure 25,000 cubits along the north, 10,000 along the sea side, and 25,000 along the south.

why: A strip 25,000 by 10,000 has four sides, and the Hebrew gives all four. The Greek names only three and has 'the mountain of the holy things' where the Hebrew has 'the sanctuary of the LORD'. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: The whole length is 25,000 and the width 10,000.
t: Ten thousand or twenty thousand in all?
p: The Hebrew total for the two strips is 10,000 wide; Swete's Greek has 20,000.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: כָּל־אֹרֶךְ חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף וְרֹחַב עֲשֶׂרֶת אֲלָפִים (kol-orekh... verochav asereth alafim)
readings.en: all the length twenty-five thousand and the width ten thousand
readings.plain: The whole length is 25,000 and the width 10,000.

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.orig: πᾶν τὸ μῆκος πέντε καὶ εἴκοσι χιλιάδες, καὶ εὖρος εἴκοσι χιλιάδες
readings.en: the whole length twenty-five thousand, and a width of twenty thousand
readings.plain: The whole length is 25,000 and the width 20,000.

why: The priests' strip (48:10) and the Levites' strip (48:13) are each 10,000 wide, so together they are 20,000, and with the 5,000 of the city (48:15) they make the 25,000 of 48:20. The Greek's 20,000 gives that sum; the Hebrew 10,000 does not. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew, and the note at 48:8 gives the other places where the Hebrew totals fail (45:1, 48:9).
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.

a: From that day on, its name will be: The LORD Is There.
t: 'The LORD Is There', or no new name?
p: Swete's Greek text printed in Swete gives no name at the end.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and the name of the city from that day: The LORD is there
readings.plain: From that day on, its name will be: The LORD Is There.

readings.w: Greek, as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (about AD 350)
readings.en: its name will be its name
readings.plain: From that day on, its name will be its name.

why: The Hebrew gives the name, and every Hebrew witness we have gives it. The Greek, as printed in Swete, has 'from the day it comes to be, its name will be its name', with no equivalent of YHWH shammah, and ends with a mark of the kind used in the Greek manuscripts to flag differences from the Hebrew. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; the name is the book's closing word.
b: No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions preserves this verse.
